questions.q: This is plain JavaScript with a typo. What does it print?
questions.explain: Reading a property that does not exist gives undefined in JavaScript. There is no error, so the bug slips through and undefined ends up in the text.

questions.q: Another typo in plain JavaScript. This time the code uses the missing value. What does it print?
questions.explain: task.titel is undefined, and calling a method on undefined throws a TypeError. JavaScript only finds this when that line runs; TypeScript would report it before running anything.

questions.q: TypeScript's checking is called static checking. What does "static" mean here?
questions.explain: The compiler tsc reads the code and its types and reports mistakes before the program ever runs. JavaScript, by contrast, finds mistakes only while the program runs.
options: The checks only run on files that never change
The code is checked without running it
The checks run while the server handles requests

questions.q: When a TypeScript program runs on Node.js, what does Node.js actually run?
questions.explain: TypeScript only adds type notes. They are removed before the code runs, by tsx, by Node's type stripping, or by compiling with tsc. What runs is ordinary JavaScript.
options: The types first, then the code
JavaScript: the same code with the types removed
A special TypeScript engine built into Node.js

questions.q: The lesson installs TypeScript with npm install -D typescript tsx @types/node. Why -D?
questions.explain: -D saves them as dev dependencies. The type checker and the runner are development tools; the finished app only needs the JavaScript.
options: It installs the packages globally for every project
They are tools used while writing code, not code the app needs to run
It downloads a smaller debug build of each package
It is required for every package in a TypeScript project

questions.q: What does "strict": true do in tsconfig.json?
questions.explain: strict switches on all of TypeScript's safety checks. The lesson says: always use it, because it is what makes TypeScript worth having. It changes checking only, not how the code runs.
options: It stops the compiler from writing any files
It makes Node.js refuse to run code with type errors
It turns on every safety check, such as "this value might be undefined"

questions.q: With "noEmit": true in tsconfig.json, what does npx tsc do?
questions.explain: noEmit means "emit nothing": tsc is only the checker, and something else (tsx or node) does the running.
options: It compiles every file into a dist folder
It only checks the types and writes no files
It runs the project, like tsx does
It deletes the .js files it wrote earlier

questions.q: Why does the lesson's tsconfig.json set "skipLibCheck": true?
questions.explain: It skips re-checking the .d.ts type files that come with packages. Your own code is still fully checked.
options: So that your own files are not checked either
The type files of installed packages were checked when published, and skipping them is faster
So that packages without types can be installed
It turns off type checking in node_modules and in src

questions.q: What does "verbatimModuleSyntax": true make you do?
questions.explain: With this setting, an import used only for types must be written import type { ... }. ZudoJS code follows this rule.
options: Write every import on its own line
Mark imports that are only types with import type
Write the .ts extension in every import path

questions.q: The project's package.json has "type": "module" and tsconfig.json has "module": "NodeNext". Which kind of modules does TypeScript produce?
questions.explain: NodeNext means "whatever Node.js does". Because package.json says "type": "module", Node.js treats the files as ES modules.
options: Browser scripts with no modules at all
Both kinds, one file for each

questions.q: In function report(task: Task): string, what is the : string at the end?
questions.explain: An annotation is a colon and a type after a name. After the parameter list, it annotates what the function returns.
options: The return type: the compiler checks that report returns a string
A default value for the function
A note that the function converts its argument to a string

questions.q: tsc prints report.ts:10:30 - error TS2551: Property 'titel' does not exist on type 'Task'. What do 10 and 30 mean?
questions.explain: The error names the file, then the line and the column. TS2551 is the error's number, which you can search for when a message is unclear.

questions.q: The typo is fixed. What does npx tsx report.ts print?
questions.explain: The type Task and the annotations are removed before running. What remains is the same JavaScript as before, now with title spelled correctly.

questions.q: None of these variables has a type annotation. What does this print?
questions.explain: TypeScript infers that title is a string, count a number and tags a string array, and checks them. At runtime, it is ordinary JavaScript.

questions.q: There are no annotations here. Which line does tsc report as a type error?
questions.explain: From let count = 0, TypeScript infers the type number. Assigning a string later is the error Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'. Inferred types are checked just like written ones.
questions.code:
let count = 0;            // line 1
count = count + 1;        // line 2
count = "none";           // line 3
const title = "Buy milk"; // line 4
options: Line 3, because count was inferred as a number
No line: without annotations nothing is checked

questions.q: What is the lesson's rule of thumb for writing types?
questions.explain: TypeScript cannot guess what callers will pass to a function, so parameters need types. Most other types are inferred from the values.
options: Annotate every variable, so nothing is left to guessing
Annotate function parameters, and let TypeScript infer the rest
Never annotate; TypeScript always infers everything

questions.q: What does npx tsx status.ts print?
questions.explain: Members of a number enum count from 0, so Todo is 0 and Done is 1. tsx generates the object for the enum; node status.ts would refuse this file.

questions.q: Which line fails with node file.ts (Node's built-in type stripping)?
questions.explain: Type stripping only deletes types. Deleting the types from the other lines leaves valid JavaScript, but an enum needs generated code, so Node.js refuses it with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX.

questions.q: Which command checks your types?
questions.explain: Only tsc checks. tsx and node remove the types and run the code, even when it has type errors.
options: All three check types before running

questions.q: Which statement about node file.ts on Node.js 24 is true?
questions.explain: Node's type stripping replaces types with spaces and runs the rest. It reads no tsconfig.json, checks nothing, supports only erasable syntax, and needs imports to name the .ts file.
options: It checks types, but only in strict mode
It ignores tsconfig.json and does not check types
It supports every TypeScript feature, including enum
It accepts import ... from "./store.js" for a file named store.ts

questions.q: For production, what does the lesson say you usually do?
questions.explain: Compiling ahead means nothing has to remove types while the server starts, and you run exactly the files you tested.
options: Run the .ts files with tsx on the server
Compile once with tsc and run the plain JavaScript with node
Run node file.ts, because it is built in
Send the .ts files to users' browsers

questions.q: You run npx tsc --noEmit false --outDir dist on a file that has a type error. What happens by default?
questions.explain: By default tsc writes output even when there are type errors. It refuses only when you set noEmitOnError. So always read what it prints.
options: No file is written until the error is fixed
It still writes the JavaScript to dist, and prints the error
It writes the file and fixes the error for you

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Types are removed before the code runs, so at runtime task is just a plain object. typeof is JavaScript, and it knows nothing about Task.

questions.q: The type says qty is a number, and tsc reports no error. What does this print?
questions.explain: The data arrived while the program runs, and it holds the string "2". Types are gone at runtime, so nothing stops it, and "2" + 1 joins text to "21". Types cannot check data that arrives at runtime.
questions.code:
const input: { qty: number } = JSON.parse('{"qty":"2"}');

console.log(input.qty + 1);
options: TypeError: qty is not a number

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The annotation is only a promise to the compiler. The real value came from JSON.parse at runtime and is the string "yes". The last lesson of this part shows how to check such data.
questions.code:
const body: { done: boolean } = JSON.parse('{"done":"yes"}');

console.log(typeof body.done);

questions.q: A backend receives a request body from a user. Why can't TypeScript's types alone guarantee its shape?
questions.explain: The compiler checks your code, not the data users send later. Data that arrives at runtime must be checked by code that runs; TypeScript and JavaScript together at the end of this part covers that.
options: Request bodies are always strings, which TypeScript cannot read
Types are removed before the code runs, and the data only arrives while it runs
TypeScript only checks code in the browser
They can, as long as strict is on

questions.q: You run a .ts file with a type error in this page's browser terminal. What happens?
questions.explain: The browser terminal removes types the same way tsx does, and checks nothing. Use npx tsc --noEmit or VS Code to see type errors.
options: The terminal shows the tsc error and does not run the code
It removes the types and runs the code; type errors show only in tsc or your editor
It refuses to run any .ts file
It fixes the type error and runs the code

questions.q: With type Task = { id: number; title: string; done: boolean }, which line does tsc accept?
questions.explain: Only c matches the type. a has a string id, b a string done, and d misspells title, so tsc reports each one.
options: const a: Task = { id: "1", title: "Buy milk", done: false };
const b: Task = { id: 1, title: "Buy milk", done: "yes" };
const c: Task = { id: 1, title: "Buy milk", done: true };
const d: Task = { id: 1, titel: "Buy milk", done: true };

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The spread { ...task, done: true } makes a new object, so the original task is not changed. TypeScript checks that the new object still matches Task.

questions.q: This file has a typo that tsc reports as Property 'titel' does not exist on type 'Task'. Fix it so the program prints #1 Buy milk (open).
questions.explain: Change task.titel to task.title. The browser terminal runs the typo without complaint and prints undefined; only tsc or your editor points at the mistake.

questions.q: This file has three type errors (the ones from the lesson's practice). Fix all three so the program prints 2 Buy milk true.
questions.explain: Make id the number 1, set done to the boolean true, and call complete with one argument. Run the unfixed code first: it prints 11 Buy milk yes, which shows how wrong types become wrong output.

questions.q: Finish summary. It gets a Task and returns its title, a colon, and done or open. The program should print Buy milk: open and then Pay rent: done.
questions.explain: Use a template literal with a ternary for the status. The return type : string makes tsc check that every path returns a string.
questions.expected:
Buy milk: open
Pay rent: done

questions.q: Add type annotations to the parameter and the return value of total (an array of numbers in, a number out), and write the body so it adds up the prices. The program should print 60.
questions.explain: Parameters are what TypeScript cannot guess, so annotate them: prices: number[]. Without it, strict mode reports Parameter 'prices' implicitly has an 'any' type. The sum variable needs no annotation; it is inferred as a number.

questions.q: Instead of an enum, this file uses a union of strings. Finish label: return Urgent for "high" and Later for "low". The program should print Urgent Later.
questions.explain: A union of strings is erasable: remove the types and you have plain JavaScript comparing strings, so it also runs with node file.ts. tsc would reject a call like label("medium").

questions.q: Finish countOpen: it gets an array of tasks and returns how many are not done. The program should print 2.
questions.explain: tasks.filter((task) => !task.done).length counts the open tasks. You did not annotate task inside the arrow function: TypeScript infers it from Task[].

questions.q: A request sends the quantity as text, so addOne gets a string. Finish it so it turns the text into a number and adds 1. The program should print 3, not 21.
questions.explain: Convert on purpose with Number(qty). Writing qty + 1 would join text and give "21", and tsc would also reject it, because the return type says number.

questions.q: Finish complete: return a new task with done set to true, without changing the original. The program should print false true.
questions.explain: The spread { ...task, done: true } copies the task and replaces done. Setting task.done = true and returning task would change the original, and print true true.

questions.q: Plain JavaScript, where an id arrived as text by mistake. What does this print?
questions.explain: JavaScript accepts the string "1" without a word, and + with a string joins text. With a Task type saying id: number, tsc would report the wrong value where it was written.
questions.code:
const task = { id: "1", title: "Buy milk" };

console.log(task.id + 1);
options: TypeError: id is not a number

questions.q: What does npx tsx priority.ts print?
questions.explain: A number enum counts from 0: Low is 0, Medium 1, High 2. tsx can run it because it generates the enum object; node priority.ts cannot.

questions.q: This file uses only erasable syntax, so node double.ts can run it. What does it print?
questions.explain: Remove : number three times and you have plain JavaScript: const limit = 10; and function double(n) { return n * 2; }. Type stripping does exactly that.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: tags is inferred as string[], so pushing "work" is allowed (pushing 42 would not be). The array has 3 items, so count becomes 3.

questions.q: The type says id is a number. What does this print?
questions.explain: The real value is the string "7", and === never matches a string with a number. The annotation did not change the data: types only exist for the compiler.
questions.code:
const input: { id: number } = JSON.parse('{"id":"7"}');

console.log(input.id === 7);
options: TypeError: id is not a number

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The object literal matches Task, so tsc accepts it. done is true, so the ternary picks "done".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: map returns a new array of titles, which TypeScript infers as string[]. Node prints strings inside arrays with single quotes.

questions.q: Write a type Book with a title (string) and a cents price (number), then finish priceLabel so it returns the title and the price in dollars with two decimals. The program should print TypeScript Basics: $12.50.
questions.explain: type Book = { title: string; cents: number } names the object shape. (book.cents / 100).toFixed(2) gives "12.50". The $ before ${ is a normal character in the text.
